title: How Credit Cards Actually Work
tagline: Billing cycles, grace periods, and the brutal 'minimum due' trap. Used right, a credit card is free 45-day money and a CIBIL-building machine. Used wrong, it's 40% debt.
summary: Billing cycle, grace period, and why paying only the minimum due is a debt trap.

sections.title: The mental model: a short-term loan you control

paragraphs: A credit card is a **revolving short-term loan**. The bank pays the merchant immediately; you owe the bank. If you repay the full amount by the due date, that loan is **interest-free**. If you don't, the bank charges punishing interest — typically **3–3.75% per month, which is ~36–45% per year.** That single fact decides whether a card is a tool or a trap.
Three terms run everything: the **billing cycle**, the **grace period**, and the **minimum due**.

blocks.caption: Spend early in the cycle and you can get up to ~45–50 interest-free days before payment is due.

items.detail: The ~30-day window in which your purchases are tallied. All spends from, say, the 1st to the 30th appear on one statement.

The gap between the statement date and the due date (~15–25 days) during which you can pay the full bill with zero interest. A purchase made on day 1 of the cycle effectively gets cycle length + grace ≈ 45–50 interest-free days.

items.term: Total Amount Due vs Minimum Amount Due
items.detail: The statement shows both. Total Amount Due is everything you owe. Minimum Amount Due is a small slice (often ~5%) the bank asks for to keep your account 'regular' — paying only this is where people get destroyed.

blocks.title: The one rule that keeps a card a tool
blocks.text: Always pay the FULL statement amount (Total Amount Due) by the due date, every single month. Do this and you never pay a rupee of interest, you build your CIBIL score, and you enjoy ~45 days of free credit. Treat the card like a debit card with a delay.

paragraphs: The 'Minimum Amount Due' line is engineered to feel safe — 'pay just ₹X to stay on track'. But paying only the minimum triggers three things at once that can spiral fast:

items.term: You lose the interest-free grace entirely
items.detail: The moment you don't pay in full, interest (~36–45% p.a.) applies to the *whole* unpaid balance, often from the date of each purchase — not just the leftover after the minimum.

items.term: New purchases get no grace either
items.detail: Until you clear the full balance, fresh spends start accruing interest immediately. The interest-free benefit is switched off.
Interest is added, then next month's interest is charged on that bigger amount. Compounding — your friend when investing — becomes your enemy here.

blocks.title: How a small slip snowballs
blocks.expression: Carry ₹50,000 at ~3.5%/month, paying only the minimum

where.meaning: covers little more than that month's interest

blocks.result: At ~42% p.a., a ₹50,000 balance accrues roughly **₹1,750 of interest in the first month alone**. Paying only the ~₹2,500 minimum barely dents the principal, so the debt can take *years* to clear and you may repay far more than you borrowed.

blocks.title: EMI conversion and cash withdrawals
blocks.text: Two more traps: (1) Converting a bill to EMI isn't free — it carries interest (often 14–18%+) plus processing fees. (2) Withdrawing CASH on a credit card is the worst move — there's no grace period at all and interest starts from day one, plus a fee. Never use a credit card at an ATM.

cheatsheet: A credit card is a revolving loan; pay in full by the due date and it's interest-free.
Billing cycle (~30 days) + grace period (~15–25 days) = up to ~45–50 interest-free days.
Paying only the Minimum Amount Due kills your grace period and triggers interest on the whole balance, including new spends.
Always pay the Total Amount Due in full — treat the card like a delayed debit card.
Never withdraw cash on a credit card (no grace, instant interest + fee); EMI conversion isn't free.

questions.prompt: Aarav's statement shows Total Amount Due ₹18,000 and Minimum Amount Due ₹900. He pays ₹900 to 'stay safe'. What actually happens?
questions.hint: What does paying the minimum do to the grace period and to the remaining balance?
answer: Paying only the ₹900 minimum means he did *not* pay in full, so he forfeits the interest-free grace. Interest (~36–45% p.a.) now applies to the remaining ~₹17,100 — often back-dated to each purchase — and any *new* purchases also start accruing interest immediately with no grace.

The minimum barely covers the interest, so the principal hardly moves. 'Staying safe' actually flips the card from a free-credit tool into a high-interest loan. The only safe payment is the **full** Total Amount Due.
keyPoints: Grace period lost; interest on full balance
Only paying in full avoids interest

questions.prompt: Aarav's billing cycle runs 1st–30th with a due date around the 18th of the next month. To maximise interest-free days on a big planned purchase, when should he buy?
questions.hint: Purchases early in a cycle get the longest runway to the due date.
answer: Right at the **start of a new billing cycle** (around the 1st). That purchase sits on the statement that closes on the 30th and isn't due until ~the 18th of the following month — giving roughly 30 days of cycle + ~18 days of grace ≈ 45–48 interest-free days. A purchase made on the 29th, just before the statement closes, gets only the ~18-day grace. Same item, very different free-credit benefit — provided he still pays in full.
keyPoints: Buy early in the cycle for max free days
Late-cycle buys get only the grace period
Benefit only holds if paid in full

questions.prompt: Why is taking a cash advance (ATM withdrawal) on a credit card considered the single worst way to use it?
questions.hint: What protection do normal purchases have that cash advances don't?
answer: Normal purchases enjoy an interest-free grace period if you pay in full. Cash advances have **no grace period at all** — interest starts accruing from the moment of withdrawal at the full ~36–45% p.a. rate — and usually carry an upfront cash-advance fee on top. There's no scenario where it's free, so it's effectively an instant high-interest loan. If you need cash, a credit card is the most expensive possible source.
keyPoints: No grace period on cash advances
Interest from day one at ~40% p.a.
Never use a credit card at an ATM
